title: Oxygen isotopes in Arctic cod (Boreogadus saida) otoliths confirm life stage–specific vertical migrations and reveal the life history implications of early ontogenetic temperature
content:
Abstract

As a key forage fish in the Arctic, Arctic cod (Boreogadus saida) plays a critical role in transferring energy in Arctic marine ecosystems. While understanding Arctic cod population dynamics within the context of a rapidly warming Arctic could provide essential information for regional conservation efforts, it remains elusive. Here, we postulate that the isotopic ratio of oxygen (18O:16O, expressed as δ18O) in otoliths can be used to reconstruct both the thermal and spatial history of Arctic cod across the Canadian Arctic and provide insights into future population dynamics. Otoliths grow throughout the life of a fish and incorporate oxygen stable isotopes proportionate to ambient concentrations following a temperature-dependent fractionation, thereby reflecting the thermal habitats utilized by Arctic cod through their lifetime. Here, we measured δ18O in otoliths from 370 Arctic cod caught across the Canadian Arctic. We derived in-situ fractionation equations inclusive of an age component, compared these with available laboratory-derived equations, and estimated ambient temperature at larval stages of fish development. We further modelled the effects of ambient temperature experienced during otolith core formation on standard length-at-age using a generalized linear model to better understand the effects of warming temperatures on Arctic cod. The results of our study confirm ontogenetic vertical migration of Arctic cod from the epipelagic layer (0–100 m) to the deeper Atlantic water mass (>100 m) within the first year of life. However, the lack of regional small-scale variation in δ18O values within deeper Atlantic waters that fish used impeded the detection of regional horizontal movements at depth based solely on this tracer. Analyses of δ18O also showed that Arctic cod experiencing warmer temperatures during early life stages are smaller around age of maturity, suggesting applicability of the temperature-size rule. Thus, the effects of increasing surface water temperatures in the Canadian Arctic could propagate through the marine food web. While oxygen isotopes in otoliths are a promising way to monitor the effects of temperature on Arctic cod growth in the Canadian Arctic, work remains to realize the full potential of this tool to identify shifts in habitat use.
